objectives: Recognize when real-time scheduling is needed.

slides.title: Scheduling, the problem statement
slides.body:
The kernel must decide which thread runs on each CPU at every moment. With $N$ runnable threads + $C$ CPUs and $N \gg C$, choosing matters.

**Cooperative scheduling**: threads voluntarily yield control. Simple; relies on threads not hogging the CPU. Used in early single-user systems + some embedded RTOS. Modern user-space coroutines (Go goroutines, Python asyncio) are cooperative — they yield on I/O await points.

**Preemptive scheduling**: kernel interrupts threads at timer ticks (typically 1-10ms) + decides whether to schedule a different one. Used by every modern multi-user OS kernel. Guarantees fairness even against uncooperative threads.

**Hybrid** (Go runtime): user-space cooperative coroutines (goroutines) multiplexed onto preemptive OS threads. Combines lightweight context switches with kernel-enforced fairness. Modern async/concurrent systems are largely this pattern.

slides.title: Linux CFS: Completely Fair Scheduler
slides.body:
Linux's default scheduler since 2.6.23. The algorithm:

Each runnable task has a **virtual runtime (vruntime)** — how much CPU it's gotten so far, weighted by its 'nice' priority. CFS picks the runnable task with the LOWEST vruntime to run next.

Result: over time, every task gets proportional CPU. A 'nice +0' task with no contenders runs continuously; with one other 'nice +0' task they alternate evenly; with a 'nice +5' task (lower priority weight) the +0 task gets ~3× the CPU.

Implementation: a red-black tree keyed on vruntime. O(log N) to find the leftmost (lowest vruntime) task. Scheduler picks it, runs for a scheduling quantum (~1-6ms depending on N), updates its vruntime, re-inserts.

Production tuning: `sched_min_granularity_ns` = minimum slice (default 750µs); `sched_latency_ns` = target latency for all runnable tasks (default 6ms). Adjusting these trades off interactive responsiveness vs throughput.

slides.title: Real-time scheduling, when CFS isn't enough
slides.body:
CFS provides *fairness*; it doesn't guarantee *deadlines*. For real-time work (audio, motion control, networking), Linux offers two real-time scheduling classes:

- **SCHED_FIFO**: a thread runs until it blocks, yields, or a higher-priority thread becomes runnable. No time-slicing among same-priority threads.
- **SCHED_RR** (round-robin): same as FIFO but time-slices among equal-priority threads.

These preempt all CFS threads. A buggy SCHED_FIFO thread that doesn't block locks out the system. Real-time scheduling is for *trustworthy* workloads — audio servers, soft-RT industrial control, network ISRs.

For hard real-time (deadline guarantees), Linux has `SCHED_DEADLINE` (CBS — Constant Bandwidth Server): each task declares (runtime, period, deadline); the kernel guarantees the runtime within the period or fails the task. Used by some automotive + industrial systems but not common in user-space apps.

Most productionapps just run on CFS + accept its statistical-fairness behavior.

question.question: Derive CFS fair-share allocation
question.goal: Two tasks: A nice=0 (weight 1024), B nice=5 (weight 335). Both runnable. CPU share?

steps.prompt: CFS allocates CPU in proportion to weight. Each task's share = its_weight / sum_of_weights. A's share?
steps.reveal: A gets 1024/1359 ≈ 75% of CPU; B gets 335/1359 ≈ 25%. So A gets ~3× B's CPU.

steps.prompt: If a third task C nice=10 (weight 110) joins, A's new share?
steps.reveal: A drops to 1024/1469 ≈ 70%. CFS smoothly re-allocates as the runnable set changes.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{CFS share}_i = w_i / \sum_j w_j}$$ Proportional fair share. nice values map to weights; each +1 nice = ~1.25× less weight (so +5 nice = ~3× less weight than +0). Fairness is over the long run; short-term latency depends on tunables.

question.question: An audio app needs to produce a sample every 23µs without dropouts. Best scheduling class:
options: SCHED_FIFO — preempts CFS; audio thread runs whenever it has work.
question.explanation: Audio has hard latency requirements. CFS guarantees fairness, not low latency. SCHED_FIFO preempts CFS; the audio thread runs immediately when it has work. JACK, PipeWire, professional audio stacks all use SCHED_FIFO. The cost: if the audio code has a bug that doesn't block/yield, the system can hang — so SCHED_FIFO requires careful audit.

hints: What scheduling class can preempt the CFS scheduler entirely?
Real-time scheduling classes (FIFO, RR, DEADLINE) sit above CFS.
slides.workedSolution: SCHED_FIFO threads run whenever runnable, preempting all CFS. Audio production: assign the audio thread SCHED_FIFO at priority ~70. Now even a busy desktop won't introduce audio dropouts. JACK, PipeWire, ALSA all do this. Caveat: misbehaving SCHED_FIFO threads can lock the system; only use for thoroughly-tested code.

question.question: Tail latency under load
question.prompt: Your gRPC service runs fine at low load; under load, p99 latency jumps from 5ms to 200ms. CPU usage is only 60%. Walk through the most likely scheduling-related cause + how you'd verify it.
Explain in two or three sentences why kernel preemptive scheduling can't be replaced by language-level cooperative coroutines in a general-purpose OS.
question.rubric: Mentions that cooperative scheduling relies on every runnable entity to yield; one uncooperative entity blocks everyone else; in a multi-user/multi-app OS you can't trust every app to yield correctly; kernel preemption forces fairness.
